topics.name: Odin
topics.kicker: Allfather of the Norse gods · Traded an eye for wisdom, father of Thor
topics.briefing: Odin ruled Asgard as the one-eyed king of the Norse gods, forever hungry for more wisdom than any god should want. He traded an eye for a single drink from a magic well, and hanged himself from the World Tree for nine nights just to learn a new alphabet. Two ravens flew across the whole world every day just to keep him informed, and even then, he knew Ragnarök would one day swallow him whole.

sample.note: the 13 real QBReader tossups for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked)

tossups.p: Disguised as the farmhand Bölverk [“BURL-vehrk”], this figure won over the giantess Gunnlöð and stole the Mead of Poetry from her father Suttung, after slithering through a hole in a mountain in the shape of a snake. He also traded one of his eyes for a single drink of wisdom from the Well of Mimir [“MEE-mir”].
tossups.r: Two ravens named Huginn and Muninn fly across the world each day and report back to him. For 10 points, name this one-eyed chief of the Norse gods, the father of Thor.

tossups.p: This figure owns a ring called Draupnir [“DROW-pnir”] that drips eight new rings of equal weight every ninth night. Dwarves forged that ring as part of a wager that also produced a golden boar and the hammer Mjölnir for his son.
tossups.r: He rides to battle on the eight-legged horse Sleipnir and keeps two wolves, Geri and Freki, fed at his feet. For 10 points, name this Allfather of Asgard, who is destined to be swallowed by the wolf Fenrir at Ragnarök.

tossups.p: With his brothers Vili and Vé, this god killed the primordial giant Ymir and built the world from his body, raising Ymir’s skull as the sky. He is also said to have won the secret of the runes by piercing himself with his own spear.
tossups.r: This husband of Frigg hung from the World Tree Yggdrasil for nine nights to learn that secret. For 10 points, name this one-eyed ruler of the Norse gods.

tossups.p: After a war between two families of gods, this figure preserved the severed head of the wise being Mimir with herbs so that it could keep advising him. He later disguised himself as a farmhand to win the Mead of Poetry from the giant Suttung.
tossups.r: This figure’s ravens, Huginn and Muninn, bring him news from across the nine worlds every day. For 10 points, name this one-eyed chief god of Norse mythology, whose son Thor wields the hammer Mjölnir.

tossups.p: Disguised as a gruff ferryman named Hárbarðr [“HAR-bard”], or “Graybeard,” this figure once traded insults with his own son and refused to row him across a strait. In another tale, disguised as a traveler, he won a riddle contest against the giant Vafþrúðnir [“vahf-THROOTH-nir”] by asking a question only he himself could answer.
tossups.r: That final, unanswerable riddle was about what he had once whispered into his dead son Baldr’s ear. For 10 points, name this chief of the Norse gods, who gave up an eye at the Well of Mimir for wisdom.

tossups.p: In the Prose Edda’s frame story, a traveler named Gangleri questions three enthroned figures called High, Just-As-High, and Third, who are later revealed to be forms of this one god. The witch Gullveig was also burned three times in this deity’s hall, helping spark a war between two families of deities.
tossups.r: His wolves, Geri and Freki, and his ravens, Huginn and Muninn, are constant companions. For 10 points, name this one-eyed king of Asgard, father of Thor.

tossups.p: This god and his brothers Vili and Vé were sons of the god Borr and the giantess Bestla. According to the Poetic Edda, he hanged himself from a windswept tree, pierced by his own spear, for nine long nights to gain knowledge of the runes.
tossups.r: He rules from his throne Hliðskjalf, from which he can see into all nine worlds. For 10 points, name this one-eyed Allfather, husband of Frigg.

tossups.p: To earn a single drink from the Well of Mimir, this figure gave up one of his own eyes, gaining great wisdom in return. He is also said to ride into battle on an eight-legged horse born to Loki, who had shapeshifted into a mare.
tossups.r: This god’s hall, Valhalla, welcomes half of all warriors who die bravely in battle. For 10 points, name this one-eyed chief of the Norse gods, father of Thor.

tossups.p: This figure’s eight-legged horse, Sleipnir, was born after Loki, disguised as a mare, distracted a giant’s stallion to stop him from finishing the walls of Asgard. This deity also kept two wolves, Geri and Freki, well fed, since he himself needed no food.
tossups.r: His ravens Huginn and Muninn bring him news from around the world each day. For 10 points, name this one-eyed Allfather, who is destined to be swallowed by the wolf Fenrir at Ragnarök.

tossups.p: Two ravens named Huginn, meaning “Thought,” and Muninn, meaning “Memory,” fly across the world each day and whisper what they see into this figure’s ears. This deity hanged himself from the World Tree Yggdrasil for nine nights, wounded by his own spear, to learn the secret of the runes.
tossups.r: He also traded one eye for a drink of wisdom from the Well of Mimir. For 10 points, name this chief of the Norse gods, husband of Frigg and father of Thor.

tossups.p: This god’s two wolves, Geri and Freki, whose names both mean something like “greedy,” eat all the food at his table, since this deity needs none himself. This one-eyed figure also won the Mead of Poetry from the giant Suttung while disguised as the farmhand Bölverk.
tossups.r: His hall of the slain, Valhalla, is filled with warriors chosen by the Valkyries. For 10 points, name this Allfather of the Norse gods.

tossups.p: Half of all warriors who die bravely in battle are chosen by the Valkyries to feast in this figure’s hall, Valhalla, until Ragnarök. This husband of Frigg once disguised himself as a ferryman to insult his own son across a strait.
tossups.r: He also traded an eye for wisdom at the Well of Mimir. For 10 points, name this one-eyed chief of the Norse gods, father of Thor.

tossups.p: At Ragnarök, this god will be swallowed whole by the giant wolf Fenrir, only for Fenrir to then be killed by this god’s own son Víðarr [“VEE-thar”]. Long before that final battle, this deity had sacrificed an eye for wisdom at the Well of Mimir.
tossups.r: His ravens Huginn and Muninn and his wolves Geri and Freki are always close by. For 10 points, name this one-eyed Allfather of Asgard.

tossups.p: This god’s eight-legged horse, Sleipnir, was actually born to Loki, who is this god’s blood brother rather than his son. This deity’s own son, by contrast, is the thunder god Thor, who wields the hammer Mjölnir.
tossups.r: This figure sacrificed an eye at the Well of Mimir and hanged himself from Yggdrasil to learn the secret of the runes. For 10 points, name this one-eyed chief of the Norse gods.

tossups.p: This deity rules from Asgard as the chief of the Norse gods, accompanied everywhere by his ravens Huginn and Muninn and his wolves Geri and Freki. He famously gave up one eye for a drink of wisdom from the Well of Mimir.
tossups.r: This god’s hall, Valhalla, welcomes fallen warriors, and his son Thor wields the hammer Mjölnir. For 10 points, name this one-eyed Allfather of the Norse gods.

trap.title: Odin, Woden, or Wotan?
trap.body: Odin, Woden, and Wotan are all the exact same god — just the Norse, Old English, and German versions of his name (that’s also why Wednesday is “Woden’s day”). Don’t mistake an unfamiliar spelling for a wrong answer. Separately, don’t confuse this chief god with his son Thor or his blood brother Loki, who share many of the same stories.
trap.fix: If a clue uses “Woden” or “Wotan,” it’s still this same god. If the clue is about a hammer or thunder, buzz Thor instead; if it’s about shapeshifting pranks, buzz Loki.
trap.line: Real answer line: Odin [or Woden; or Wotan]

topics.name: Loki
topics.kicker: Norse trickster god · Caused Baldr’s death, bound until Ragnarök
topics.briefing: Loki was the Norse gods’ favorite troublemaker, a shapeshifter clever enough to solve the problems he caused and sneaky enough to cause most of them in the first place. He once turned into a mare and gave birth to an eight-legged horse, and on a darker day, he tricked a blind god into killing his own brother. For that final betrayal, the other gods bound Loki with his own son’s chains until the day he breaks free to help end the world at Ragnarök.

sample.note: the 7 real QBReader tossups for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked)

tossups.p: After secretly shaving off the golden hair of the goddess Sif, this god made amends by convincing the Sons of Ivaldi to forge her a magical replacement out of real gold. He then bet his own head with the dwarf Brokkr that Brokkr’s brother could not out-craft that first set of gifts.
tossups.r: A fly bite from this meddling god during the forging gave the hammer Mjölnir its unusually short handle. For 10 points, name this Norse trickster god.

tossups.p: To stop a giant builder from finishing the walls of Asgard on time, this deity transformed into a mare and lured away the builder’s stallion, Svaðilfari [“svah-THIL-far-ee”]. This trickster later gave birth to an eight-legged foal from that encounter.
tossups.r: That foal, Sleipnir, became Odin’s horse. For 10 points, name this shapeshifting Norse god, who is also the father of the wolf Fenrir.

tossups.p: This figure tricked the blind god Höðr [“HUH-thur”] into throwing a dart made of mistletoe, the one plant that could harm Höðr’s brother. That brother had seemed invulnerable because every other object in creation had sworn an oath never to hurt him.
tossups.r: For his role in the death of that beloved god, Baldr, this figure was hunted down and bound with the entrails of his own son. For 10 points, name this Norse trickster god.

tossups.p: As punishment for a crime against another god, this figure was bound to three stones with the entrails of his son Narfi, which the gods turned into iron chains. His wife Sigyn sits beside him, catching venom from a serpent in a bowl so that it will not drip on his face.
tossups.r: He will break free at Ragnarök to kill, and be killed by, the watchman god Heimdallr. For 10 points, name this bound Norse trickster god.

tossups.p: After insulting every god at a feast, this figure fled and hid as a salmon in a waterfall called Franang’s Falls. The gods caught him using a net modeled on one he himself had foolishly invented while hiding.
tossups.r: He was then bound with his own son’s entrails as punishment for his role in the death of the god Baldr. For 10 points, name this shapeshifting Norse trickster god.

tossups.p: At a feast hosted by the sea giant Ægir [“EYE-year”], this figure killed a servant named Fimafeng and then traded savage insults with every god and goddess present, in a poem called the _Lokasenna_ [“LOH-kah-SEN-ah”]. He was driven out only after threatening to burn the hall down.
tossups.r: He also disguised himself as a handmaid to help Thor sneak into a giant’s hall and recover a stolen hammer. For 10 points, name this Norse trickster god.

tossups.p: To make the giantess Skaði [“SKAH-thee”] laugh as repayment for her father’s death, this figure tied himself to a goat with a cord and staged a ridiculous tug-of-war. He had caused that death earlier by tricking the giant Þjazi [“THYAH-zee”] into chasing him while he carried off the goddess Iðunn [“IH-dun”].
tossups.r: This mischievous god also shaved off the golden hair of Thor’s wife, Sif, as a prank. For 10 points, name this Norse trickster god.

tossups.p: Disguised as an old woman named Þökk [“THOHK”], meaning “Thanks,” this figure alone refused to weep for a dead god, dooming him to stay in the underworld instead of returning to the living. That trick kept the beloved god Baldr dead for good.
tossups.r: This deity’s own daughter, Hel, rules over that same underworld. For 10 points, name this Norse trickster god.

tossups.p: This god’s father was the giant Fárbauti [“far-BOW-tee”], and his wife is the loyal goddess Sigyn [“SIG-in”]. Through his lover, the giantess Angrboða [“ANG-gur-boh-tha”], he fathered three monstrous children.
tossups.r: Those children include the wolf Fenrir and the serpent Jörmungandr. For 10 points, name this Norse trickster god, the blood brother of Odin.

tossups.p: With the giantess Angrboða, this figure fathered the wolf Fenrir, the serpent Jörmungandr, and Hel, ruler of the underworld. At Ragnarök, Fenrir will swallow Odin while Jörmungandr poisons Thor, fulfilling this family’s grim destiny.
tossups.r: This same god will fight and kill the watchman Heimdallr before dying himself. For 10 points, name this father of monsters, a Norse trickster god.

tossups.p: Disguised as a handmaid alongside Thor, who wore a wedding dress and veil, this figure helped trick the giant Þrymr [“THRIM”] into returning a stolen hammer. He had earlier helped discover the theft by borrowing Freyja’s feathered cloak to fly in search of it.
tossups.r: This shapeshifter is also blamed for cutting off the golden hair of Thor’s wife, Sif. For 10 points, name this trickster god of Norse mythology.

tossups.p: This deity will kill, and be killed by, the ever-watchful god Heimdallr at Ragnarök. Before that final battle, he spends years bound beneath the earth with a serpent dripping venom onto his face, caught by his faithful wife Sigyn in a bowl.
tossups.r: He is blamed for tricking the blind god Höðr into killing the beloved god Baldr. For 10 points, name this bound Norse trickster god.

tossups.p: This shapeshifting god once turned into a mare to distract a stallion named Svaðilfari, later giving birth to the eight-legged horse Sleipnir. On another occasion, he turned into a fly to sabotage the forging of the hammer Mjölnir.
tossups.r: He is more infamous for tricking Höðr into killing the god Baldr with mistletoe. For 10 points, name this Norse trickster god, father of the wolf Fenrir.

tossups.p: This figure’s children include a wolf destined to kill Odin, a serpent destined to kill Thor, and a daughter who rules the land of the dishonorable dead. This blood brother of Odin often travels with the gods despite causing most of their problems.
tossups.r: He will be bound with his own son’s entrails until Ragnarök. For 10 points, name this trickster god, responsible for the death of Baldr.

tossups.p: This Norse god’s constant shapeshifting and scheming eventually caused the death of the beloved god Baldr, for which the other gods bound him with his own son’s entrails. His wife Sigyn stayed by his side, catching dripping venom in a bowl.
tossups.r: He will break free at Ragnarök to kill, and be killed by, Heimdallr. For 10 points, name this trickster god, the father of Fenrir, Jörmungandr, and Hel.

topics.name: Thor
topics.kicker: Norse god of thunder · Wields Mjolnir, dies fighting the world serpent
topics.briefing: Thor was the Norse gods’ head-first solution to almost every giant problem, a short-tempered thunder god who swung a hammer that always flew back to his hand. He fished for the world-ending serpent Jormungandr, got tricked into wrestling old age itself, and once put on a wedding dress to win his hammer back from a giant groom. Thursday is still named for him, and Norse myths agreed that he and Jormungandr were fated to kill each other at Ragnarok.

tossups.p: While visiting the hall of the giant king Utgard-Loki, this god failed to empty a drinking horn secretly connected to the sea and lost a wrestling match against an old woman who was actually Old Age itself. He also failed to lift a housecat off the floor, not realizing it was really the world serpent in disguise.
tossups.r: That serpent, Jörmungandr, is fated to kill, and be killed by, this god at Ragnarök. For 10 points, name this Norse god of thunder.

tossups.p: After the giant Þrymr stole this god’s hammer and demanded the goddess Freyja as ransom, this god dressed as Freyja himself, with his companion Loki posing as a handmaid, to sneak into the giant’s hall and reclaim it. At the wedding feast, he nearly gave himself away by eating a whole ox and eight salmon.
tossups.r: Once the hammer was back in his hands, he used it to kill Þrymr and the other wedding guests. For 10 points, name this Norse god of thunder, son of Odin.

tossups.p: This god once went fishing with the giant Hymir, using an ox’s head as bait to hook the world serpent, Jörmungandr. Just as he was about to kill the serpent with his hammer, a terrified Hymir cut the fishing line.
tossups.r: This god and that same serpent are destined to kill each other at Ragnarök. For 10 points, name this Norse god of thunder, husband of the golden-haired Sif.

tossups.p: To keep the clever dwarf Alvíss from marrying his daughter Þrúð, this god kept the dwarf talking with riddle after riddle until sunrise turned him to stone, since dwarves could not survive daylight.
tossups.r: This same god wields a hammer forged by the dwarf brothers Brokkr and Eitri. For 10 points, name this Norse god of thunder, son of Odin.

tossups.p: A fly bit the eyelid of the bellows-working dwarf Brokkr while he and his brother Eitri forged this god’s favorite weapon, giving it an unusually short handle. The fly was secretly Loki, trying to sabotage a bet over whose dwarven creations were better.
tossups.r: Despite its short handle, that hammer, Mjölnir, always returns to this god’s hand when thrown. For 10 points, name this Norse god of thunder.

tossups.p: This god owns a magical belt called Megingjörð that doubles his already great strength, along with a pair of iron gloves called Járngreipr that let him safely grip red-hot metal and his own hammer.
tossups.r: These treasures go along with his hammer, which always returns to his hand when thrown. For 10 points, name this Norse god of thunder, son of Odin.

tossups.p: This god’s chariot is pulled by two goats, Tanngrisnir and Tanngnjóstr, whom he can slaughter and eat for a meal and then resurrect good as new the next morning using their hides and bones.
tossups.r: Those same goats carried him to feasts among the giants. For 10 points, name this Norse god of thunder, wielder of the hammer Mjölnir.

tossups.p: At the god Baldr’s funeral, this deity grew so annoyed with a dwarf named Litr getting underfoot that he kicked the dwarf straight into the funeral pyre. He had been blessing the pyre with his hammer at the time.
tossups.r: This god is the son of Odin and the wielder of the hammer Mjölnir. For 10 points, name this Norse god of thunder.

tossups.p: After Loki shaved off all of the hair of this god’s wife, Sif, as a cruel prank, this god forced Loki to visit the dwarven Sons of Ivaldi and have them forge a head of real gold hair that would grow like natural hair.
tossups.r: That same trip resulted in several other treasures for the gods, including this god’s own hammer, Mjölnir. For 10 points, name this Norse god of thunder, son of Odin.

tossups.p: This god’s mother is the giantess Jörð, whose name simply means “Earth,” making this deity’s stepmother the goddess Frigg. Despite having a giant for a mother, he becomes one of the giants’ fiercest enemies.
tossups.r: This son of Odin wields the hammer Mjölnir. For 10 points, name this Norse god of thunder.

tossups.p: After this god dies fighting the world serpent Jörmungandr at Ragnarök, his sons Móði and Magni are said to inherit his hammer and survive into the new world. Their names mean “Wrath” and “Might.”
tossups.r: Their father wielded that hammer, Mjölnir, as the Norse god of thunder. For 10 points, name this son of Odin.

tossups.p: In a duel against the stone giant Hrungnir, this god’s hammer shattered his opponent’s thrown whetstone, but a shard of that stone stayed lodged in this god’s head for the rest of his life. The seeress Gróa later tried to chant it loose but forgot her spells after hearing happy news.
tossups.r: This god usually fares better against giants with the help of his hammer, Mjölnir. For 10 points, name this Norse god of thunder, son of Odin.

tossups.p: To reach the hall of the giant Geirröd safely, this god borrowed a magic staff, belt, and iron gloves from a helpful giantess named Gríðr. With that gear, he caught and threw back a piece of red-hot iron that Geirröd had hurled at him.
tossups.r: This same god more famously owns his own belt of strength and his own iron gloves to go with his hammer. For 10 points, name this Norse god of thunder.

tossups.p: This god is fated to kill the world serpent Jörmungandr at Ragnarök, only to die moments later from its poison. His wife is the golden-haired goddess Sif, whom the trickster Loki once pranked by shaving off all her hair.
tossups.r: This son of Odin wields a hammer that always returns to his hand when thrown. For 10 points, name this Norse god of thunder.

tossups.p: Thursday takes its name from this deity in Old English, much as Wednesday takes its name from this deity’s father. This short-tempered god is destined to kill, and be killed by, the serpent Jörmungandr at the final battle of Ragnarök.
tossups.r: He wields a hammer called Mjölnir that always returns when thrown. For 10 points, name this Norse god of thunder, son of Odin.

topics.briefing: Heracles was the strongest hero in Greek mythology, a son of Zeus who was forced to complete Twelve Labors after the goddess Hera drove him into a fit of madness. Theseus became king of Athens himself, but a single forgotten detail, the color of his ship’s sails, convinced his own father that he had died.

tossups.r: This hero had better luck than Medea hoped, later sailing to Crete and defeating an even more dangerous bull-headed monster. For 10 points, name this slayer of the Minotaur.

tossups.p: Before setting out for Athens, this hero lifted a boulder to find the sword and sandals his father had hidden there as a test. His mother, Aethra [“EE-thruh”], had raised him alone in Troezen [“TREE-zen”] and finally told him who his father was.
tossups.r: Using those as proof, this hero was recognized by his father, the king of Athens. For 10 points, name this hero who went on to kill the Minotaur.

tossups.p: After being freed from the Underworld’s “Chair of Forgetfulness,” this hero was said to have left behind part of his own backside, which Athenian comedians later joked explained why Athenians had unusually small backsides. His friend Pirithous was not so lucky and remained stuck forever.
tossups.r: This hero had gone to the Underworld to help Pirithous try to kidnap Persephone. For 10 points, name this Greek hero who slew the Minotaur.

tossups.p: This hero defeated the bandit Sinis, the “Pine-Bender,” by tying him between two bent pine trees, the same trap Sinis had used on travelers. This hero also pushed the cliffside robber Sciron into the sea.
tossups.r: This hero defeated such villains on his way to Athens, where his father ruled as king. For 10 points, name this Greek hero who killed the Minotaur using thread from Ariadne.

trap.title: Theseus or Heracles?
trap.body: Theseus and Heracles are often tangled together: Heracles rescues Theseus from the Chair of Forgetfulness in the Underworld (but cannot also free Theseus’s friend Pirithous), and both heroes deal with a famous bull (Theseus kills the Minotaur; Heracles captures the Cretan/Marathonian Bull). A clue about being rescued from the Underworld, or about black-and-white sails, or about Ariadne’s thread, means Theseus, not Heracles.
trap.fix: Listen for who is doing the action. If the hero needs help from someone else, such as being saved by Heracles or guided by Ariadne’s thread, the answer is usually Theseus. If the hero is doing Twelve Labors himself, it is Heracles.

topics.name: Gilgamesh
topics.kicker: Hero-king of Uruk · Star of the oldest surviving epic in the world
topics.briefing: Gilgamesh was a Sumerian king so strong that the gods made him a best friend, Enkidu, just to keep him in line — and the plan backfired when the two became inseparable instead. After Enkidu died, a terrified Gilgamesh crossed the known world searching for eternal life, even meeting Utnapishtim, a man who had survived a flood much like Noah’s. His adventures, written on clay tablets in Mesopotamia thousands of years ago, make up the oldest great epic that still survives today.

trap.title: The hero or the poem?
trap.body: Gilgamesh the character and _The Epic of Gilgamesh_ the poem are two different real answer lines. Clues about “this man,” “this king,” or “this hero” want Gilgamesh. Clues about “this text,” “this poem,” or an opening line like “Surpassing all other kings” want the epic itself, even though the two share almost every clue.
trap.fix: Listen for the noun right before the clue, the same trick that separates a person from their namesake book or war. If it says “this text” or describes the poem being written or titled, say the epic. If it says “this man” or “this king,” say Gilgamesh.

topics.name: Quetzalcoatl
topics.kicker: Aztec feathered-serpent god · Linked to wind, learning, and Venus
topics.dates: Worshipped across Mesoamerica for over 1,000 years
topics.briefing: Quetzalcoatl was the feathered-serpent god the Aztecs credited with creating humankind by grinding up old bones and mixing them with his own blood. He was linked to the wind, learning, and the planet Venus, and he feuded endlessly with his rival, Tezcatlipoca. According to a legend written down after the Spanish conquest, the Aztec ruler Moctezuma II mistook the conquistador Hernán Cortés for this god returning home — though many historians today doubt that story is true.

trap.title: Quetzalcoatl or Tezcatlipoca?
trap.body: These two rival gods appear together in almost every real tossup, so a clue about one often sits right next to a clue about the other. Tezcatlipoca (“Smoking Mirror”) is linked to night, jaguars, and sacrifice; Quetzalcoatl is the feathered serpent linked to wind, learning, and Venus. The rival is usually the one doing the tricking — he shames Quetzalcoatl into drunkenness and self-exile, not the other way around.

topics.name: Horus
topics.kicker: Falcon-headed Egyptian sky god · Son of Osiris and Isis
topics.briefing: Horus was the falcon-headed god of the sky, so important to the ancient Egyptians that every pharaoh was said to rule as his living form on earth. After his uncle Set murdered his father, Osiris, young Horus fought Set for eighty years to win back the throne — and lost an eye in the struggle, giving rise to the famous protective symbol known as the Eye of Horus. He finally won, becoming king of Egypt and avenging his father.

trap.title: Horus or Osiris?
trap.body: Horus and his father Osiris are both central to the same story, so clues about one can sound like clues about the other. Osiris clues describe a murdered, mummified king who becomes ruler of the underworld. Horus clues describe the falcon-headed son who avenges him and wins the throne of the living. Their shared enemy, Set (also spelled Seth), is Osiris’s brother and Horus’s uncle — never the hero of either story.
trap.fix: If the clues describe a death, a mummy, or ruling the underworld, it is Osiris. If they describe the wedjat eye, a falcon, a boat race, or defeating Set, it is Horus.

tossups.p: Homer calls this warrior “swift-footed” throughout one epic poem. The god Hephaestus [“heh-FESS-tus”] forged this man a new shield decorated with images of the earth, sun, moon, and stars after his old armor was lost.
tossups.r: That old armor had been worn by his best friend, Patroclus, when Hector killed him in battle. For 10 points, name this Greek hero of the Trojan War, who avenged Patroclus by killing Hector.

tossups.p: Zeus himself reportedly wanted to marry this man’s mother until a prophecy warned that her son would grow greater than his own father. This man’s father, Peleus [“PEE-lee-us”], later led him to command the Myrmidon soldiers of Thessaly.
tossups.r: His mother, the sea nymph Thetis, dipped him in the River Styx as a baby, leaving only his heel unprotected. For 10 points, name this hero killed by an arrow from Paris.

tossups.p: This man killed the Ethiopian king Memnon, son of the dawn goddess Eos, whose grieving soldiers were turned into birds. He had earlier killed a Greek soldier named Thersites [“thur-SY-teez”] for mocking him over his grief for a fallen Amazon.
tossups.r: That Amazon queen, Penthesilea [“pen-thuh-suh-LEE-uh”], had been killed by this man in battle. For 10 points, name this Greek hero whose only weak spot was his heel.

tossups.p: This man once wounded King Telephus [“TEL-eh-fus”] of Mysia with his spear, then later healed that same wound using rust scraped from the spear’s blade. He also killed the Amazon warrior Penthesilea, then mourned over her body.
tossups.r: His mother had dipped him in the River Styx as a baby, protecting every part of him except his heel. For 10 points, name this Greek hero killed by Paris’s arrow.

tossups.p: Some myths claim that after his death, this man married the sorceress Medea in the afterlife. Earlier in his life, he clogged a river with enemy corpses, prompting the river god Scamander [“skuh-MAN-der”] to try to drown him.
tossups.r: The god Hephaestus drove the river back with fire to save him. For 10 points, name this Greek hero of the Trojan War, later killed by an arrow to his heel.

tossups.p: This man once nearly killed the Trojan prince Aeneas in single combat, until the sea god Poseidon swept Aeneas away to safety. This man’s rage at the start of one epic poem is aimed at his own commander, Agamemnon, who had taken his captive, Briseis [“bry-SEE-is”].
tossups.r: He refused to fight again until his best friend, Patroclus, was killed while wearing his armor. For 10 points, name this Greek hero who then killed Hector in revenge.

tossups.p: To keep him out of the Trojan War, this man’s mother disguised him as a girl at the court of King Lycomedes [“ly-koh-MEE-deez”] on the island of Skyros. He gave himself away by instinctively grabbing a sword hidden among a pile of jewelry, and he had a son, Neoptolemus [“nee-op-TOL-eh-mus”], with the princess Deidamia [“day-ih-duh-MY-uh”] there.
tossups.r: He later became the greatest Greek warrior at Troy. For 10 points, name this hero whose only vulnerable spot was his heel.

tossups.p: An ancient epic poem opens with an invocation asking a muse to sing of this man’s “rage,” sparked when his commander, Agamemnon, seized his captive woman, Briseis. This man refused to fight for the Greeks until his closest friend was killed.
tossups.r: That friend, Patroclus, died while wearing this man’s own armor. For 10 points, name this Greek hero who then killed Hector and dragged his body behind his chariot.

tossups.p: After this man’s death, Odysseus and Ajax argued bitterly over who deserved to inherit his armor, and Ajax took his own life after losing the contest. This man’s remains were said to have been mixed together with those of his closest friend after both died in the war.
tossups.r: That friend, Patroclus, had died wearing this man’s armor. For 10 points, name this Greek hero killed by an arrow to his only weak spot, his heel.

tossups.p: This man killed the Amazon queen Penthesilea during the war, then was said to have grieved over her body. After his own death soon after, Ajax and Odysseus quarreled over who should receive his famous armor.
tossups.r: That armor had been forged by Hephaestus to replace the armor Hector took from his best friend, Patroclus. For 10 points, name this Greek hero of the Trojan War.

tossups.p: This man once fought the river Scamander after clogging it with the bodies of enemies he had killed, nearly drowning before the fire god Hephaestus drove the river back. This man killed the soldier Thersites for insulting his grief over a fallen Amazon warrior.
tossups.r: He had earlier refused to fight after Agamemnon took his captive, Briseis. For 10 points, name this Greek hero who was finally killed by an arrow to his heel.

tossups.p: This son of Peleus and the sea nymph Thetis hid at the court of King Lycomedes before the war began, disguised in women’s clothing. While there, he had a child, Neoptolemus, with the princess Deidamia.
tossups.r: He went on to lead the Myrmidon soldiers against Troy. For 10 points, name this Greek hero who was dipped in the River Styx as a baby, leaving only his heel vulnerable.

tossups.p: The god Hephaestus forged a famous shield for this man, decorated with images of the whole cosmos, after his original armor was lost in battle. Some later myths claim that this man married the sorceress Medea in the afterlife.
tossups.r: He had earlier avenged his friend Patroclus by killing the Trojan prince Hector. For 10 points, name this Greek hero whose mother dipped him in the River Styx as a baby.

tossups.p: This man briefly dueled the Trojan prince Aeneas before the god Poseidon rescued his opponent from the fight. This man later killed Memnon, the son of the dawn goddess Eos, whose Ethiopian soldiers mourned by turning into birds.
tossups.r: This man was eventually killed by an arrow that struck the one unprotected part of his body, his heel. For 10 points, name this Greek hero who killed Hector to avenge Patroclus.

tossups.p: This man was the greatest warrior to fight for the Greeks in the Trojan War, famous for his terrifying battle rage. An ancient epic poem opens by invoking a muse to sing of that very rage, provoked when Agamemnon took away his captive woman, Briseis.
tossups.r: He refused to fight until the death of his beloved friend Patroclus brought him back into battle to kill Hector. For 10 points, name this hero whose mother dipped him in the River Styx, missing only his heel.

trap.title: Which name is the answer?
trap.body: Achilles tossups are crowded with other characters: Patroclus, Hector, Paris, Agamemnon, Ajax, and Odysseus all show up as supporting players, not answers. It is easy to blurt out “Hector” when a clue describes Hector’s body being dragged around Troy, since Hector is the one the action happens to — but the question is asking about the man doing the dragging.
trap.fix: Track the pronoun “this man” or “this hero” all the way through the clue, not whichever name you heard most recently. The answer is whoever that pronoun points to, not the last person mentioned.
